questions.question: At the top price, Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited's P/E is 10.7x. Similar listed companies have a P/E of about 31.4x. What does that tell you?

choices.text: It costs about the same as, or less than, similar companies for each rupee of profit.
It costs more than similar companies for each rupee of profit, so its profit must grow faster to be worth it.
The P/E shows how many shares the company has.

questions.explanation: A P/E of 10.7x against 31.4x means you pay no more for each rupee of Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited's profit than for its peers'. That is a fair starting point, not a guarantee.

questions.question: Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited owes 2.78 rupees of loans for every rupee of its owners' money. Which is closest to the truth?

choices.text: Its loans are small to manageable next to what the owners have put in.
Its loans are heavy: lenders have more riding on it than its owners.
Loans never matter for a company that makes a profit.

questions.explanation: At 2.78 rupees of loans per rupee of owners' money, lenders have more riding on Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited than its owners, and repayments are due even in bad years.

questions.question: Insiders paid ₹88 a share on average. You would pay ₹82. What does the gap mean?

choices.text: Insiders got a much better deal, so be sure the business is worth your higher price.
The company will pay you back the difference.
The price band must be a mistake.

questions.explanation: At 0.93x what insiders paid, you pay close to their price for Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited: a good sign.

questions.question: An unofficial grey market premium of ₹7 a share is being quoted. How much should you rely on it?

choices.text: Completely: it tells you the listing price.
A little at most: it is unregulated and easy to push around.
It is set by the stock exchange.

questions.explanation: The grey market premium of ₹7 for Bombay Coated and Special Steels Limited is gossip with a number on it: nobody regulates it, and it often turns out wrong.
